_comment: A pit: a funnel of loose ground sunk into the surface. The one member of the geometric family that
goes DOWN -- rings, obelisks and pyramids all stand on the ground, and this is cut into it.
**A cone with its tip below its base**, which is the whole shape. `Cone` reads `tipY < baseY` as
pointing down, so the mouth is the widest part and it narrows as it deepens -- what a pit looks like,
and the reason this is a cone rather than the half-ellipsoid a bowl would be.
**Heights are measured from the ground's top block**, `sunk` making 0 that block rather than the one
above it, so the mouth IS the surface -- what makes what the pit is made of something you can walk
onto, and what the scarab medallion reads as exposed (design §7.1.2). Sizes and poses scale about 0,
so it stays flush at every size.
**`sunk`, so it is dug in the way vanilla's surface lake is.** The mouth sits on the LOWEST ground
under it and the ground standing higher is cut away, so on a slope the pit is a hollow with a bank
on its uphill side instead of standing proud of the ground below; a site too steep to cut is
refused, as a lake refuses one its bowl would be open to.
**Warped, then undulated, then clipped at the mouth**, and each does one thing. Warping moves the
outline sideways, so the footprint is lobed rather than a circle -- undulating alone never changes
which columns a cone covers, which is why the first pits read as perfect. Undulating makes the floor
uneven. The clip keeps any column the undulation lifted from standing proud of the mouth.
About sixteen across as written, between a landmark and a puddle (Jonah, 2026-09-23), and one to a
64-block cell, so `colossal` is a pond-sized one and `tiny` a puddle.
